title: Data
text: The eSIM gives 30GB at full speed, then slows right down. Use hotel wifi for photo backups. See How-to 2.

title: Umbrellas and wet gear
text: Use the umbrella stand or the plastic sleeve at shop doors. Clear umbrellas are cheap at any convenience store. Pack a light rain jacket each.

title: Power
text: A power bank and a USB-C cable each. Charge phones, power banks and AirPods every night.

title: Maps on luggage days
text: Turn on the accessible or step-free route option in the maps app. It finds the lifts and avoids stairs.

title: Luggage and lockers
text: Coin lockers at every big station take Suica. Large sizes fill by mid morning, so use a staffed counter for suitcases. Before any bag is handed over, take out passports, wallets, chargers and medication.

title: Creased clothes
text: Convenience stores and Don Quijote sell wrinkle release spray (シワ取りスプレー). Spray, smooth with your hands and hang for a few minutes. Easier than finding an iron.

title: Trains
text: Phones on silent, no calls, bags off your back in a crowd. Queue on the platform markings and let people off first.

title: Crowded trains
text: Carry hand sanitiser. A mask is useful if you prefer one in crowded indoor spaces.

title: Escalators
text: Stand on the left in Tokyo, on the right in Osaka, and on the right in Hong Kong.

title: Crossing
text: Wait for the green man, even on an empty street. Nobody jaywalks.

title: Taxi doors
text: The rear left door opens and closes by itself in Japan. Leave it alone.

title: Cash and coins
text: About ¥5,000 to ¥10,000 each a day is plenty. Small restaurants, market stalls, temple entry and shrine charms are often cash only. Keep a coin purse of ¥10, ¥50, ¥100 and ¥500 for machines and temples. Top up as you go: 7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart and Japan Post ATMs take foreign cards, most with English.

title: The right mix of yen
text: Notes are ¥1,000, ¥5,000 and ¥10,000. Keep three or four ¥1,000s each for stalls, temples and taxis; break ¥10,000s at convenience stores, not small shops. ATMs give mostly ¥10,000s, so ask for an amount like ¥19,000 to get smaller notes. Most useful coins: ¥100 and ¥500 for machines, a few ¥10 and ¥5 for shrines.

title: Cards and cash
text: Carry two cards, kept separately. Leave one card and some emergency cash in the room safe. Never keep both phones, wallets and cards in one bag. If an ATM or card machine offers to charge you in AUD, choose yen.

title: Money tray
text: Put cash or card on the small tray at the till, not into the hand. Change comes back the same way.

title: No tipping in Japan
text: Not expected anywhere, and it can cause confusion. A thank you is enough.

title: Ticket machine restaurants
text: Many ramen and casual places have a machine at the door. Pick, pay, then hand the ticket to the staff.

title: Eating and walking
text: Eat at the stall or standing to one side, not on the move. Same on local trains, other than the Shinkansen. A lidded takeaway coffee on the go is fine in the city, but markets and temple lanes often ask you not to, so stand aside there. Bins are rare, so plan to carry the cup.

title: Chopsticks
text: Never stand them upright in rice or pass food from chopstick to chopstick. Rest them on the holder.

title: Litter
text: Public bins are rare. Carry a small bag and take rubbish back to the hotel or a convenience store.

title: Cold lockers
text: Some stations and department stores have refrigerated lockers. Ask for an ice pack when buying food to carry.

title: Passports
text: Carry the physical passports on shopping days: Sat 17, Mon 19, Thu 22 and Sun 25. A photo on the phone is not accepted for tax-free.

title: Fitting rooms
text: Put on the thin face cover (フェイスカバー) the shop gives you before pulling on a top, so makeup does not mark the clothes. Shoes off at the fitting room step.

title: Tax-free
text: Japan's tax is already in the price. Spend ¥5,000 or more before tax in one store, show your physical passports, and the tax isn't charged: you save the 10% tax on most goods (8% on take-away food and soft drinks), about 9% and 7% off the shelf price. Food bought tax-free goes in a sealed bag: keep it sealed until you leave Japan. See How-to 4.

title: No fakes into Japan
text: Since October 2022, bringing counterfeit or replica branded goods into Japan is illegal even for personal use, in your luggage or by post. That covers bags, watches, shoes and clothing. Customs can seize and destroy them on arrival, with no compensation. Leave any knockoffs at home. The vintage luxury stores sell authenticated pieces, so keep the receipts.

title: Street Kart
text: Wear fully closed shoes. Take the physical licence card, the physical International Driving Permit and passports. Photos are not accepted.

title: Shrines and temples
text: Bow once at the torii gate and walk to the side of the path, not down the middle. Rinse hands at the basin. At a shrine: bow twice, clap twice, bow once. At a temple, no clapping.

title: The ¥5 coin
text: Called go-en, which also means "good connection", so it is the lucky offering at a shrine. Keep a few aside.

title: Bowing
text: A small nod back is all that is needed.

title: Shoes and socks
text: Shoes come off wherever there is a step up or a rack at the door: temples, some restaurants, fitting rooms. Wear good socks, and carry a clean spare pair on temple and shrine days.

title: Nara deer
text: Buy the crackers, show empty hands when you run out, and keep maps and paper out of reach. They bow, and they also nip.

title: Geisha and maiko
text: No photos in Gion without permission, and keep off the private lanes. There are fines.

title: Massage
text: A head spa, foot or body massage near each hotel is listed in How-to 21. Book head spas a day or two ahead.

title: Hong Kong: cash
text: Octopus covers trains, buses and most shops. For cash, carry HK$20, HK$50 and HK$100 notes. Taxis and small stalls often cannot change HK$500 or HK$1,000. Some red taxis are still cash only.

title: Hong Kong: tipping
text: Restaurants add 10% service. Round up for taxis. Small notes for porters.

title: Hong Kong: MTR
text: No eating or drinking past the gates. There are fines.

title: Hong Kong: trams
text: Board at the back, pay with Octopus at the front as you get off. Upper deck, front seat.
